corrections.before: Before checking any Vast.ai-specific services, confirm the host machine has a stable, working internet connection with outbound access. Run each check below and compare your output with the expected result.

corrections.before: This command asks your DNS server to translate the domain name `vast.ai` into an IP address. The host daemon connects to Vast.ai servers by domain name, so even with a working internet connection, the machine cannot reach Vast.ai if DNS resolution is broken.

corrections.before: - **`active (running)`** is the healthy state — the service started successfully and is currently running. Any other state (`inactive (dead)`, `failed`, `activating (auto-restart)`) means the service is not running normally.
corrections.after: - **`active (running)`** means systemd currently considers the service running. It does not establish that the daemon can reach Vast.ai or use every GPU. If the state is `inactive (dead)`, `failed`, or `activating (auto-restart)`, inspect the status details and recent logs to determine what happened.

corrections.before: - **A very recent start time is a warning sign.** If you run `systemctl status vastai` repeatedly and the "ago" value keeps resetting to a few seconds or minutes (and the `Main PID` keeps changing), the service is crashing and being restarted over and over — a **restart loop**. The state `activating (auto-restart)` with a message like `Restart=on-failure` or `Scheduled restart job` also indicates a restart loop. In that case, inspect the logs (see the debugging commands below) to find the crash reason.
corrections.after: - **Repeated recent starts deserve investigation.** If the "ago" value repeatedly resets and the `Main PID` changes, the service is restarting. A single `activating (auto-restart)` state or `Scheduled restart job` message is not enough to establish a loop. Check several observations and the recent logs for exits, timeouts, manual actions or other restart causes; do not assume every restart is a crash.

corrections.before: This command shows the NVIDIA driver status and every GPU the operating system currently sees, including temperature, power, and memory usage. The Vastai service requires all GPUs to be visible at this level — if the driver cannot see them, the service will fail to start.
corrections.after: This command shows NVIDIA driver information and status fields for GPUs available through that driver, including supported temperature, power and memory readings. Compare the listed GPUs with those you expect on the host. Missing GPUs or driver errors need investigation; this output alone does not establish whether the Vastai service can start.

corrections.before: Expected result (your GPU model, driver version, and values will differ):
corrections.after: Illustrative output format, not a captured result for your host. Your GPU model, driver version, supported fields and values will differ:

corrections.before: What to look for: a table listing **every GPU installed in the machine**, each with a valid name, temperature, and memory reading. Signs that something is wrong:
corrections.after: What to look for: the GPUs you expect to be available through the NVIDIA driver, with their names and supported readings. `N/A` can be normal for an unsupported field. Investigate unexpected missing devices or errors using the checks below:

corrections.before: - **Fewer GPUs listed than physically installed** — a GPU has dropped off the PCIe bus (power, riser, or slot issue) or has a hardware fault.
corrections.after: - **Fewer GPUs listed than expected** — investigate device visibility, driver/module configuration, power and PCIe connectivity. The count alone does not identify the cause or prove a hardware fault.

corrections.before: - **`ERR!` or `Unknown Error` in any column** — the GPU is in a faulty state and may need further diagnosis.
corrections.after: - **`ERR!` or `Unknown Error` in a field** — record the exact message and inspect the driver and kernel logs. An error reading does not by itself establish a hardware fault.

corrections.before: - **The command hangs for a long time** — usually indicates a GPU stuck on the bus or a driver-level problem.
corrections.after: - **The command hangs or takes unusually long** — record when it happens and inspect the driver and kernel logs. The delay alone does not identify the underlying cause.

corrections.before: Start the service manually. If it was simply stopped, this brings it back up; if it fails immediately, the error message points you to the cause:
corrections.after: Attempt to start the service, then check the command result and service status. If it does not start or stops again, inspect the recent logs for the reason:

corrections.before: Show a detailed per-GPU report from the driver (much more detail than plain `nvidia-smi`), including ECC error counters, throttle reasons, and PCIe link status — useful for spotting a GPU that is detected but unhealthy:
corrections.after: Show a detailed per-GPU report from the driver, including supported ECC, clock-event or throttle, and PCIe fields. Unsupported fields may show `N/A`. Use the readings with the logs when investigating a detected GPU; the report alone does not establish overall health:

corrections.before: Search the kernel ring buffer for NVIDIA driver errors (`NVRM`, `Xid`) and PCIe/AER bus errors with human-readable timestamps. `Xid` messages are NVIDIA's hardware/driver error codes and often reveal why a GPU fell off the bus:
corrections.after: Search the kernel ring buffer for NVIDIA (`NVRM`, `Xid`) and PCIe/AER messages. `dmesg -T` shows human-readable timestamps, which can be inaccurate after suspend/resume. Xid messages are NVIDIA driver error reports and provide starting points for investigation; they do not always identify a single root cause:

corrections.before: Common root causes include NVIDIA driver errors, GPU power/PCIe issues, BIOS configuration changes, or a recent kernel/OS update.
corrections.after: Possible areas to investigate include NVIDIA driver state, GPU power and PCIe connectivity, BIOS configuration, and recent kernel or OS changes.

corrections.before:
This page has two paths. **Full system upgrade** is the shorter route for a
machine you already keep current, and it patches the kernel along with
everything else. **Kernel-only upgrade** moves the kernel and leaves the rest of
the system where it is. Neither moves Ubuntu to a newer version, for example
22.04 to 24.04.
corrections.after: This page has two paths. **Full system upgrade** considers available updates for installed packages. **Kernel-focused upgrade** targets the installed kernel metapackages and any dependencies APT needs. Review the proposed changes in either case. With package sources configured for your current Ubuntu release, these commands update its packages; they do not run a release upgrade such as 22.04 to 24.04.

corrections.before:
An up-to-date kernel is one requirement out of several. On its own it does not
mean the machine will pass verification. Ubuntu also releases updates for the
rest of the system. The full system upgrade installs those as well; the
kernel-only path leaves them alone.
corrections.after: A security-patched kernel is one requirement out of several and does not by itself establish verification. The full system upgrade considers updates across installed packages. The kernel-focused path requests the selected kernel metapackages, but dependencies can change too; review APT’s complete proposed changes.

corrections.before:
A kernel upgrade only takes effect after a reboot, and a reboot stops every
running instance on the machine. Instances are not destroyed, but the workloads
inside them are interrupted. Do not start until you have a maintenance
window. Wait until all active rental contracts have ended, or schedule the
window with
[`vastai schedule maint`](/cli/reference/schedule-maint) so renters are
notified and can save their work.
corrections.after: Booting an updated kernel normally requires a reboot, which interrupts running workloads. Before starting, review rental and storage commitments and arrange a maintenance window when the hardware is not actively being used. Schedule the window with [`vastai schedule maint`](/cli/reference/schedule-maint) so renters receive the planned-maintenance notice and can prepare.

corrections.before:
For a machine whose packages you already keep current. The kernel moves with
everything else, and the whole upgrade is three commands:
corrections.after: For a machine whose package changes you are prepared to review. Run the three commands below one at a time, checking each result before continuing. Stop on errors, and reboot only after confirming that the intended kernel update was installed.

corrections.before:
This is a full system upgrade, not a kernel upgrade. Every package with an
update available moves inside the same maintenance window, services are
restarted as part of it, and a machine that misbehaves afterwards leaves you the
whole upgrade to work back through rather than a single change.
corrections.after: This operation can upgrade packages across the system, not just the kernel. APT may keep some packages back, and package scripts may restart services. Review the full change list and keep its output so you can investigate problems after the upgrade.

corrections.before:
Take this path only if you know what it will change on your machine and can put
it right yourself if something breaks. To move the kernel on its own, use the
kernel-only path below.
corrections.after: Take this path when you have reviewed APT’s proposed changes and have a recovery plan. To focus the request on kernel metapackages, use the path below and still review its dependency changes.

corrections.before:
`--with-new-pkgs` is not optional here. A kernel upgrade pulls in new versioned
packages such as `linux-image-5.15.0-190-generic`, and plain `apt-get upgrade`
will not install packages that are not already present, so it holds the kernel
back:
corrections.after: Use `--with-new-pkgs` in this upgrade command. When a kernel metapackage needs new versioned dependencies, such as a new `linux-image-...` package, plain `apt-get upgrade` does not install them and can keep the metapackage back:

corrections.before:
The machine then reboots onto the kernel it was already running.
`--with-new-pkgs` allows those additions, and it never removes a package.
corrections.after: If the intended kernel update was kept back, do not assume the reboot applied it. `--with-new-pkgs` allows new dependency packages during `upgrade` without allowing removals; check the installed and running kernel versions afterward.

corrections.before:
Differing values mean GRUB booted the old kernel. See
[If the machine booted the old kernel](#if-the-machine-booted-the-old-kernel).
corrections.after: If the running release differs from the kernel you intended to boot, inspect the installed kernel files and GRUB menu. A different kernel family can also explain the comparison. See [If the machine booted the old kernel](#if-the-machine-booted-the-old-kernel).

corrections.before:
`nvidia-smi` does not substitute for that check. When GRUB boots the old kernel,
the DKMS module built against that kernel is still in place, so `nvidia-smi`
lists every GPU on a machine that never took the patch. Comparing the running
kernel against the newest one in `/boot` is what catches it.
corrections.after: `nvidia-smi` checks GPU-driver visibility, not which kernel booted. It can succeed under an older kernel with a compatible driver. Use `uname -r` to compare the running release with the kernel you intended to install, and check GPU visibility separately.

corrections.before:
For a machine where you want the kernel to move on its own and the rest of the
system to stay where it is. The five steps below query the metapackage names
rather than assuming them, install the update, and confirm it took.
corrections.after: Use this path to focus the upgrade request on your installed kernel metapackages. The steps query their names, review available candidates and dependency changes, request the upgrade, and compare the installed and running versions.

corrections.before: On a machine running the GA kernel:
corrections.after: Example output when `linux-generic` is installed:

corrections.before: On a machine running the HWE kernel:
corrections.after: Example output when the queried HWE metapackage is installed:

corrections.before:
This is why the names are queried rather than hardcoded. On an HWE machine
`linux-generic` is not installed, and passing it to the upgrade command in step
3 reports success while patching nothing:
corrections.after: Query the installed names rather than assuming them. If `linux-generic` is not installed, passing that name with `--only-upgrade` skips it instead of installing or upgrading your HWE metapackage:

corrections.before:
The command exits `0`, so nothing looks wrong. This is the one step that can
leave you with an inaccurate record: the machine is still on its old kernel, but
the run looks like it succeeded. Step 5 is what catches it.
corrections.after: An otherwise successful command can exit `0` after skipping a package, so the exit status alone does not prove a kernel update occurred. Check the selected metapackage versions and the running kernel in Step 5.

corrections.before:
If `Installed` and `Candidate` are the same, the machine is already at the
current patch level and step 3 has nothing to do. That is the normal result of a
routine check. Before calling it done, confirm the kernel you are running is the
newest one installed, since an earlier upgrade may be installed but never
rebooted into:
corrections.after: If `Installed` and `Candidate` match for every selected metapackage, the current APT cache proposes no version change for those packages. Confirm that the metadata refresh succeeded and the configured sources are correct. Then compare the running kernel with the release you intended to boot; an earlier update may have been installed without being booted:

corrections.before:
Matching values mean the machine is up to date and running what it should. Note
the version and the date and you are done. Differing values mean the newer
kernel is installed but not booted, so the machine needs the reboot in step 4
but not the install in step 3.
corrections.after: If the running release matches the intended updated kernel and the selected metapackages have the expected installed versions, record the version and date. If the intended kernel is installed but not running, investigate the boot selection and plan the reboot in Step 4; do not repeat the package install solely because the release strings differ.

corrections.before:
If they differ, `Candidate` is the version you are about to install, and the
remaining steps need a maintenance window.
corrections.after: If the selected metapackage has a different available `Candidate`, review APT’s proposed version and dependency changes before accepting the install. Complete the remaining disruptive steps within your maintenance window.

corrections.before:
Upgrade the metapackage, not a bare `linux-image-...` package. The metapackage
depends on both the image and the matching headers, which is why
`linux-headers-5.15.0-190-generic` appears above. DKMS needs headers matching
the kernel it is building for, and the NVIDIA driver is built by DKMS. Install
an image on its own and the driver has nothing to rebuild against, so the GPUs
disappear on the next boot.
corrections.after: Use the appropriate kernel metapackage so its matching image and header dependencies are considered together. For DKMS-built NVIDIA modules, the target kernel needs matching headers. Ubuntu also supplies precompiled NVIDIA modules for supported kernels. Confirm that the chosen driver-module path supports the kernel you intend to boot before restarting.

corrections.before:
This stops every running instance on the machine. Before you run it, confirm
you are inside your maintenance window and that there are no active rentals.
corrections.after: A reboot interrupts running workloads. Before running it, confirm the maintenance window, review existing rental and storage commitments, and ensure the hardware is not actively being used.

corrections.before:
If the first line is older, the machine booted the previous kernel and the
upgrade has not taken effect. See
[If the machine booted the old kernel](#if-the-machine-booted-the-old-kernel).
corrections.after: If `uname -r` reports an older release than the updated kernel you intended to boot, investigate why that entry was not selected. See [If the machine booted the old kernel](#if-the-machine-booted-the-old-kernel).

corrections.before:
When `uname -r` matches the newest kernel in `/boot`, `Installed` matches
`Candidate`, and `nvidia-smi` lists every GPU, the machine is up to date for its
release and back in service. Record the new kernel version and the date against
the machine for your own maintenance log; the next check reads the current state
from `apt-cache policy` rather than from that record.
corrections.after: When the intended kernel is running, the selected metapackages have the expected versions, and the expected GPUs are visible, record the kernel version and date in your maintenance log. Before returning to service, also check the services, storage and connectivity affected by the maintenance. The next package check reads the current APT state rather than relying on the log.

corrections.after: If the machine is reachable over SSH, begin by inspecting the kernel files and boot configuration remotely. Keep console access available in case a later repair or reboot requires it.

corrections.before:
Two values break it. `GRUB_DEFAULT=saved` boots whatever booted last, and
paired with `GRUB_SAVEDEFAULT=true` every boot re-saves the old kernel as the
default, so the machine stays on it through any number of upgrades. A
`GRUB_DEFAULT` pinned to one entry, by index or by title, boots that kernel and
ignores newer ones:
corrections.after: `GRUB_DEFAULT=saved` selects the saved menu entry. With `GRUB_SAVEDEFAULT=true`, selecting an entry can save it for later boots; an explicitly saved or version-specific entry can therefore keep selecting an older kernel. A numeric index selects that position in the generated menu, so inspect the actual entries rather than assuming it always names one kernel:

corrections.before:
If the new kernel is absent, stop here and do not reboot. This output is the
menu that was just generated, so a menu still missing the kernel is not
something re-running `update-grub` will change, and rebooting only lands you on
the old kernel again. Absence means `grub-mkconfig` did not find the kernel to
begin with: check that `/boot` is mounted and that
`/boot/vmlinuz-<version>` and the matching `/boot/initrd.img-<version>` both
exist for the version you installed.
corrections.after: If the intended kernel or its menu entry is missing, stop and inspect the generation errors and actual GRUB menu before rebooting. Check that `/boot` is mounted and that the expected `/boot/vmlinuz-<version>` and `/boot/initrd.img-<version>` files exist. Correct the cause, regenerate the menu, and verify the intended entry before proceeding.

corrections.before:
That gets the machine running again on the old kernel. The new kernel is still
installed, so work out why it failed before rebooting into it again.
corrections.after: If the previous kernel boots successfully, keep the machine on it while investigating why the intended kernel failed. The newer kernel files can remain installed; do not select them again until you understand the failure. If neither entry boots, use the console error output to continue diagnosis.

corrections.before:
If the machine boots but `nvidia-smi` reports
`NVIDIA-SMI has failed because it couldn't communicate with the NVIDIA driver`,
the GPU driver did not rebuild for the new kernel. The machine will show as
offline and cannot take rentals. See
[Offline Machine](/host/machine-offline), which covers that symptom.
corrections.after: If the machine boots but `nvidia-smi` reports `NVIDIA-SMI has failed because it couldn't communicate with the NVIDIA driver`, inspect the module and kernel logs. A missing or failed-to-load module, driver conflict or module-signing problem can cause this message; it does not by itself prove a DKMS rebuild failure. See [Offline Machine](/host/machine-offline) for the next diagnostic checks.
